## Review

::: {.takeaway}
Test MSE is the quantity we want. One train and test split estimates it noisily,
and costs us data.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.question}
You split `Auto` in half on Friday. What happens with a different split?
:::
:::

## Limitations {.small}

::: {.incremental}
1. The estimate depends heavily on which split was drawn  
2. Fitting on a subset overstates the error of the deployed model  
:::

# LOOCV {.center}

## LOOCV

![](img/islp/fig5_3.png){fig-align="center" width="76%"}

::: {.source}
ISLP Figure 5.3. Each observation takes a turn as a validation set of size one.
:::

```{python}
#| output: asis
#| echo: false
iterative_latex(
    "LOOCV",
    r"\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{MSE}_i",
    highlights=[
        r"\text{MSE}_i",
        r"\sum_{i=1}^{n}",
        r"\frac{1}{n}",
    ],
    explanations=[
        "The MSE from the single fold where observation $i$ was held out and every other observation trained the model.",
        "Add that leave-one-out MSE up over all $n$ observations, since each gets a turn.",
        "Divide by $n$ to average it, exactly like training or test MSE.",
    ],
)
```

## k-fold cross-validation

![](img/islp/fig5_5.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.source}
ISLP Figure 5.5. Five fold cross-validation. Each fifth takes a turn as the
validation set.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\text{MSE}_j$$
:::

## Choosing k {.small}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### LOOCV

Low bias, since each fit uses $n-1$ points.

High variance, since the $n$ fits are nearly identical and their errors are
correlated.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### $k = 5$ or $k = 10$

A little bias.

Lower variance.

$k$ fits rather than $n$.
:::

::::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.takeaway}
Bias and variance, applied to the estimator itself.
:::
:::

# In Python {.center}

## cross_val_score {.small}

```{python}
DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LucyMcGowan/sta-363-f26/main/data/"
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold  # <1>
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

Auto = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Auto.csv")
X = Auto[["horsepower"]]
y = Auto["mpg"]

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(2), LinearRegression())  # <2>
cv = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=363)  # <3>
scores = -cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")  # <4>
scores.round(2)
```
1. `cross_val_score` runs the whole cross-validation loop, fitting and
   scoring once per fold; `KFold` is the object that defines how the folds
   are built.
2. `make_pipeline` chains `StandardScaler()`, `PolynomialFeatures(2)`
   (degree 2 polynomial terms of `horsepower`), and `LinearRegression()`
   into one estimator, assigned to `model`.
3. `KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=363)` builds 10 folds;
   `shuffle=True` randomizes row order before splitting, and
   `random_state=363` fixes that shuffle.
4. `cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")`
   returns one score per fold. scikit-learn's scorers are defined so that
   higher is better, so MSE is reported negative; the leading `-` flips it
   back to ordinary (positive) MSE, assigned to `scores`.

## Stability of 10-fold CV {.small}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
degrees = range(1, 11)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.5))
for r in range(9):
    cv_r = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r)
    curve = [
        -cross_val_score(
            make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression()),
            X, y, cv=cv_r, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
        ).mean()
        for d in degrees
    ]
    ax.plot(degrees, curve, color="#d5008f", alpha=0.55, lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Polynomial degree")
ax.set_ylabel("10-fold CV MSE")
ax.set_ylim(15, 28)
plt.show()
```

::: {.source}
Nine runs of 10-fold CV on `Auto`, differing only in the fold assignment.
:::

## CV for classification

::: {.takeaway}
Replace MSE with the error rate. Nothing else changes.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{python}
#| eval: false
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy")  # <1>
```
1. The only change from the regression call above is `scoring="accuracy"`
   in place of `scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"`; `model`, `X`, `y`, and
   `cv` are reused exactly as defined earlier.
:::
